name: Ayodhya Kanda
title: Ayodhya Kanda: Rama’s Exile and Bharata’s Choice
description: A detailed Ayodhya Kanda guide covering Kaikeyi’s demands, Rama’s exile, Dasharatha’s death, Bharata’s appeal and the sandals, with sarga references.
dek: The city prepares to celebrate its future king. Before the ceremony can begin, a promise changes the lives of an entire family.
summary: Ayodhya Kanda follows the collapse of Rama’s planned installation, his departure with Sita and Lakshmana, Dasharatha’s death and Bharata’s effort to bring him home. Rama keeps the exile, while Bharata governs on his behalf with Rama’s sandals as the sign of his authority.
editionNote: References follow K. M. K. Murthy’s 119-sarga Ayodhya Kanda at ValmikiRamayan.net. The chapter ranges below are reading aids; they are not a claim that every edition divides the narrative identically.

sections.heading: A coronation that seems to unite everyone
paragraphs: Dasharatha sees Rama as a suitable heir and seeks the support of the assembled leaders. Rama’s qualities are presented through his conduct toward other people: his learning, self-control, attentiveness and ability to protect the kingdom. The succession appears to join the king’s wish with public approval.

Preparations fill Ayodhya. Rama and Sita undertake the disciplines associated with the ceremony. The speed of the arrangements, the king’s anxieties and the absence of Bharata create a situation that is outwardly joyful but vulnerable to a sudden change.
Beginning with celebration gives the exile its force. Rama is not wandering because he has failed to win a kingdom; he is asked to relinquish a position that is already within reach.

sections.heading: Manthara, Kaikeyi and the two demands
paragraphs: Manthara persuades Kaikeyi to see Rama’s installation as a danger to Bharata and to her own position. Kaikeyi’s reaction changes during their exchange. Her earlier affection for Rama should remain visible when reading the severity of the decision she eventually makes.

Kaikeyi invokes two boons Dasharatha has promised her. She demands Bharata’s installation and fourteen years of forest exile for Rama. Dasharatha is devastated but cannot easily escape the pledge by which she binds him. Several chapters dwell on the argument and the suffering of the king rather than rushing directly to Rama’s departure.

The received narrative here does not require a divine possession of Manthara to explain events. Accounts that give the gods a different role must be attributed to their own traditions. The immediate action turns on persuasion, fear, a royal promise and the use of that promise.

sections.heading: Rama accepts exile; Sita and Lakshmana insist on joining
paragraphs: Rama accepts the demand as an obligation connected with his father’s word. This does not mean everyone agrees with him. Kausalya grieves and Lakshmana is angry at the injustice. Rama has to explain his decision in the presence of people whose love takes the form of resistance.

Sita is initially told to remain in Ayodhya. She argues for accompanying her husband and refuses to let his description of forest hardships decide the matter for her. Their exchange gives her a clear voice in the decision to leave. She is not an object silently carried from palace to forest.

Lakshmana also insists on accompanying them. His role will combine protection, practical labour, affection and difficult obedience. The three travellers leave for the same destination, but each arrives at that decision through a different relationship to duty.

sections.heading: What leaving Ayodhya costs
paragraphs: Rama distributes wealth before departing. The palace scenes include the changing of clothes, leave-taking, appeals to Kaikeyi and the grief of the queens. Sita’s encounter with bark garments makes the change in circumstance physically visible.

The people follow the departing chariot. Rama eventually leaves them behind as they sleep, preventing their loyalty from drawing the city into the exile with him. The journey crosses rivers and passes through the territory of Guha, whose hospitality gives the travellers a new form of shelter outside the royal household.

Guha and Lakshmana keep watch; Sumantra must eventually return. At Bharadwaja’s hermitage the travellers receive directions to Chitrakuta, where they establish a dwelling. The forest contains hospitality, beauty and the possibility of a life together, even while Ayodhya remains in grief.

sections.heading: Dasharatha remembers an earlier act of violence
paragraphs: Sumantra returns with news and messages. Comfort does not erase the king’s anguish. Dasharatha recalls a hunting incident in which he killed a young ascetic after mistaking the sound of water for an animal. He had to carry the news to the young man’s blind parents.

The father’s curse connects Dasharatha’s present suffering with the loss he once caused another household. The narrative makes him face not only separation from his own son but the memory of another parent’s bereavement. His death leaves the kingdom without a ruler while the intended heir is absent.
The ministers and sages turn to the problem of succession. Public order cannot be suspended indefinitely because a family is grieving. Bharata and Shatrughna must be summoned home.

sections.heading: Bharata refuses the benefit obtained in his name
paragraphs: Bharata returns from his maternal relatives without having engineered the plot. The atmosphere of Ayodhya is his first warning. Learning of his father’s death and Rama’s exile, he rejects Kaikeyi’s expectation that he will welcome the throne.

His anger does not end the consequences of what she has done. He must establish his innocence before Kausalya, participate in mourning and respond to those who want him to rule. Shatrughna’s treatment of Manthara also brings the question of retaliation into the household.

Bharata decides to bring Rama back. His conduct gives the book a second example of refusing royal advantage: Rama will not seize power by setting aside his father’s word, and Bharata will not accept power won through his brother’s removal.

sections.heading: The meeting at Chitrakuta
paragraphs: Bharata sets out with the queens, attendants and a large following. Their approach causes suspicion. Guha needs to understand Bharata’s intentions, and Lakshmana initially reads the approaching force as a threat. The reader knows that a crowd can express grief and loyalty as well as aggression.

The meeting reunites the brothers without resolving the succession. Rama learns of Dasharatha’s death and mourns him. The family’s reunion takes place around a loss that cannot be reversed even if the political dispute were settled.

Rama’s questions to Bharata about administration, especially in sarga 100, extend the conversation beyond family affection. Ministers, justice, security, resources and the care of subjects belong to the responsibilities of kingship. A good intention is not sufficient preparation to govern.

sections.heading: Why Rama does not return, and why the sandals matter
paragraphs: Bharata argues that Rama should rule. Other voices enter the debate, including Jabali and Vasishta. Jabali challenges the reasoning that binds Rama to the exile, while Vasishta brings lineage and obligation into the discussion. The book preserves a dispute about the reasons for action, not just an announcement of the hero’s decision.

Rama maintains that the promised exile must be completed. Bharata receives his sandals and carries them back as the sign of Rama’s authority. He establishes himself at Nandigrama and takes responsibility for the kingdom without treating Rama’s absence as a permanent transfer of the throne.

The sandals are therefore connected with a concrete political arrangement and an emotional vow. Their later devotional importance grows from the story of a brother who accepts responsibility while refusing possession.

sections.heading: The book continues beyond Bharata’s departure
paragraphs: Ayodhya Kanda does not end at the famous meeting of the brothers. Rama leaves Chitrakuta as the conditions around the hermitages change. The travellers visit Atri and Anasuya, and Sita speaks with Anasuya about marriage and her own past.

Anasuya’s instruction reflects the ideals voiced within that ancient narrative setting. Sita’s account adds her own remembered experience to the discussion. The closing movement carries the family farther from Ayodhya and prepares the sustained forest narrative of Aranya Kanda.
For the eventual homecoming, continue to [Yuddha Kanda](/ramayana/yuddha-kanda). Its reunion with Bharata completes a promise that remains painfully open here.

questions.question: Did Bharata ask Kaikeyi to exile Rama?
questions.answer: No. In this account he is away when the demands are made. On returning, he rejects the arrangement and seeks Rama’s restoration.

questions.question: Why does Sita go into exile?
questions.answer: Sita insists on accompanying Rama after he initially proposes that she remain in Ayodhya. Their sustained exchange is in sargas 26–30.

questions.question: Does Ayodhya Kanda end with Rama becoming king?
questions.answer: No. Rama remains in exile. Bharata governs on his behalf, and the book closes with the travellers continuing into the forest.
